headline: Washington's Unlikely Venture Fund: Rare Earths, Chips, and the State as Shareholder
lede: The Trump administration has quietly assembled a government equity portfolio worth tens of billions, betting taxpayer dollars on rare-earth miners and a resurgent Intel. The returns have been extraordinary — and the precedents, troubling.
body:
When the Department of Defense agreed in July 2025 to buy $400 million of preferred stock in **MP Materials** — the Mountain Pass, California miner that is America's only operating rare-earth processing facility — it was doing something the federal government had not done outside wartime or financial crisis: taking an ownership stake in a private company as a matter of industrial policy. The Pentagon's stake, convertible into roughly 15 percent of MP's common shares, made it the company's largest single shareholder. Within a single trading session, MP's stock surged more than 50 percent. By the end of 2025 the shares had risen more than 276 percent from their pre-deal price.

The rationale was strategic rather than financial. China controls an estimated 60 to 70 percent of global rare-earth mining and a far larger share of the *processing* capacity — the energy-intensive chemical separations that turn ore into the neodymium-iron-boron magnets used in electric motors, wind turbines, and missile guidance systems. American dependence on that supply chain had been a recognised vulnerability for years; the Trump administration decided to address it with something blunter than subsidies: equity. The Defense Department also struck a deal with **Vulcan Elements**, a startup building domestic magnet manufacturing, and the Commerce Department took a stake in **USA Rare Earth**, an Oklahoma company, via a $1.6 billion package announced in January 2026.

The administration's biggest single bet, however, is on semiconductors. In August 2025 the Commerce Department converted $8.9 billion of outstanding CHIPS Act grants and Secure Enclave programme awards into 433 million shares of **Intel** common stock — a 9.9 percent ownership stake at $20.47 per share. The terms were notably passive: no board seat, no governance rights, no veto over strategic decisions. Intel's share price at the time of writing sits near $96, implying the government's position is worth roughly $41–43 billion, a paper gain of some $34 billion on an $8.9 billion outlay. That figure dwarfs anything a standard sovereign wealth fund would boast about in a single position.

The tweet that prompted this brief claims the portfolio is "up $11.6 billion in six months." That specific figure has not been independently verified by major financial outlets, and the arithmetic is slippery: the government's cost basis, the timing of each stake acquisition, and whether warrants are counted at intrinsic or market value all affect the calculation. What *is* documented is that a basket tracked by the financial data firm Insiderwave under the label "Trump Administration portfolio" showed gains of roughly 169 percent year-to-date as of October 2025, and that the portfolio grew from approximately $9.4 billion to more than $17 billion over the same period — implying paper gains in that range, though the Intel stake's subsequent moonshot has since pushed implied gains far higher. The $11.6 billion figure is plausible as a snapshot from a particular date, but readers should treat it as illustrative rather than audited.

The political-economy debate is harder to dismiss. Free-market critics argue that government equity stakes distort capital allocation — companies that win federal favour gain an implicit guarantee that crowds out competitors and suppresses the creative destruction that makes markets work. A more pointed concern comes from corporate governance specialists: even "passive" government ownership can chill strategic decisions, deter acquirers, and create conflicts when regulators oversee companies in which they are also shareholders. Intel itself flagged in an SEC filing that the government stake "may substantially limit the company's ability to pursue potential future strategic transactions." Bernie Sanders, in a rare moment of alignment with the administration, applauded the Intel deal — which perhaps illustrates that when industrial policy succeeds financially, ideological objections tend to quiet down.

History offers some precedent. The government took large stakes in General Motors and Citigroup during the 2008–09 financial crisis, eventually exiting at a modest profit and a notable loss, respectively. Those were emergency measures designed to be temporary. What is novel about the current programme is its *deliberateness*: these are not rescues but investments, made in peacetime, through multiple agencies, with no clear sunset. Whether Washington is building a sovereign wealth fund by accident, a new model of industrial policy by design, or simply a portfolio that will look very different after the next market correction remains the open question.

concepts.definition: A group of 17 metallic elements — including neodymium, dysprosium, and cerium — used in magnets, batteries, electronics, and defence systems. Despite the name, most are not geologically rare; the bottleneck is processing capacity, which China dominates.

A 2022 US law that appropriated $52 billion to revive domestic semiconductor manufacturing, primarily through grants and loans to companies building or expanding US fabs. The Trump administration converted some outstanding grant commitments into equity stakes rather than cash disbursements.

Government intervention to shape the structure of an economy — picking sectors or firms to support via subsidies, tariffs, loans, or, increasingly, direct equity investment. Long associated with East Asian development models, it has recently gained bipartisan acceptance in the United States.

A state-owned investment fund that deploys national savings or resource revenues into financial assets, typically equities and bonds. Norway's Government Pension Fund and Singapore's GIC are canonical examples. The US has no formal equivalent, though the accumulation of government equity stakes is beginning to resemble one in practice.

A 1950 US law that grants the President broad authority to direct industrial production for national security purposes, including requiring companies to prioritise government contracts and fast-tracking financing for strategic suppliers.

fact_check: The tweet's claim of '$11.6 billion' in gains over six months is unverified by major outlets. Documented figures show the tracked government portfolio grew from roughly $9.4 billion to over $17 billion (~$7.6 billion gain) through October 2025, and the Intel stake alone had risen to ~$43 billion by May 2026. A six-month window ending at a different point could produce a figure near $11.6 billion, but no authoritative source has confirmed that specific number. The '167% in 6 months' return figure is broadly consistent with the ~169% YTD figure reported by Insiderwave as of October 2025. The tweet's framing conflates percentage return with absolute dollar gain without specifying the denominator (total invested capital), which makes precision impossible without the full cost-basis data.
